explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, meets Adonijah, Solomon's older brother, with “Do you come in peace?” and he answers, “Yes, in peace.” (1 Kings 2:13) I think she's being careful with him, and I'd be careful too.

explanations.answer: Does the king know you are here
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a bouncer at the door, but it's not what she says. Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, asks Adonijah, Solomon's older brother, just one thing: “Do you come in peace?” Adonijah answers, “Yes, in peace.” (1 Kings 2:13)

explanations.answer: Why have you come to me
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since that's what I'd want to know too. But Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, goes straight to a different question: “Do you come in peace?” Adonijah, Solomon's older brother, says, “Yes, in peace,” and then tells her he has something to say. (1 Kings 2:13-14)
Yep. Adonijah says the kingship “has come to him from the LORD.” (1 Kings 2:15) He still says it was his and all Israel expected him to reign, but he says out loud where it came from.
Not quite, friend. Adonijah does say all Israel expected him to reign, but then he says the kingship came to Solomon “from the LORD.” (1 Kings 2:15) He doesn't say the people handed it over.
Not this time. Adonijah never says the army gave Solomon anything. He says the kingship “has come to him from the LORD.” (1 Kings 2:15)

explanations.answer: Abishag the Shunammite as his wife
explanations.explanation: That's it. Adonijah says, “Let him give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife.” (1 Kings 2:17) Abishag is the young woman who cared for King David in his old age (1 Kings 1:1-4).

explanations.answer: Command over the king's whole army
explanations.explanation: Big ask, but that's not what he wants. Adonijah asks for Abishag the Shunammite as his wife. (1 Kings 2:17) Nothing in his request mentions the army.

explanations.answer: A city of his own to rule over
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Adonijah's request has no city in it. He asks Bathsheba to get Solomon to give him Abishag the Shunammite as his wife. (1 Kings 2:17)

True! The text says, “The king stood up to greet her, bowed to her, and sat down on his throne.” (1 Kings 2:19) The king himself gets up when his mother walks in. Respect like that is worth a whole tray of cookies.
It's actually true. The text says Solomon stood up to greet Bathsheba and bowed to her before he sat down on his throne. (1 Kings 2:19) He didn't stay in his seat.

explanations.answer: A throne at his right hand
explanations.explanation: Right on. “The king had a throne brought for his mother, who sat down at his right hand.” (1 Kings 2:19) A whole throne, friend. That's no folding chair.
Not quite. No footstool shows up here. The king has a throne brought for his mother, and she sits at his right hand. (1 Kings 2:19)
Close to the room, but not the spot. Solomon doesn't put his mother among the officials. He has a throne brought in for her, and she sits down at his right hand. (1 Kings 2:19)

Not quite, friend. Before she says a word about what she wants, Solomon tells her, “Make your request, my mother, for I will not deny you.” (1 Kings 2:20) He says yes first. That's like signing the contract before you read it.
Right, it's false. Solomon says, “Make your request, my mother, for I will not deny you.” (1 Kings 2:20) He promises up front, before he's heard a thing. I think that's going to matter in a minute.
Yes. Solomon says, “you might as well request the kingdom for him…” (1 Kings 2:22) He hears the request for Abishag as a lot bigger than it sounds.
Not this one. The word Solomon uses is “kingdom.” He says, “you might as well request the kingdom for him…” (1 Kings 2:22)
Not quite, friend. Solomon doesn't mention a temple here. He says his mother might as well request “the kingdom” for Adonijah. (1 Kings 2:22)

That's the pair. Solomon says to request the kingdom “for him and for Abiathar the priest and for Joab son of Zeruiah!” (1 Kings 2:22) Joab was a commander in David's army. Both men backed Adonijah when he tried to make himself king. (1 Kings 1:7)
Not those two, friend. Solomon names Abiathar the priest and Joab son of Zeruiah. (1 Kings 2:22) They're the ones who stood with Adonijah. (1 Kings 1:7)
Not quite. Solomon says Abiathar the priest and Joab son of Zeruiah. (1 Kings 2:22) Those two backed Adonijah when he tried to make himself king. (1 Kings 1:7)

True. Solomon calls the LORD “the One who established me, who set me on the throne of my father David, and who founded for me a dynasty as He promised.” (1 Kings 2:24) That's a long swear, and every piece of it points back to the LORD.
It's actually true. Right in his oath, Solomon says the LORD “founded for me a dynasty as He promised.” (1 Kings 2:24) He also says the LORD set him on the throne of his father David.

explanations.answer: He carried the ark before David
explanations.explanation: Yep. Solomon tells Abiathar the priest he's sparing him “since you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before my father David, and you suffered through all that my father suffered.” (1 Kings 2:26) That's the reason the text gives.

explanations.answer: He begged the king for mercy
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The text never shows Abiathar begging. Solomon gives his own reason: Abiathar carried the ark of the Lord GOD before David and suffered through all that David suffered. (1 Kings 2:26)

explanations.answer: Zadok the priest spoke for him
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but no. The text doesn't say anyone speaks up for Abiathar. Solomon's reason is that Abiathar carried the ark of the Lord GOD before his father David. (1 Kings 2:26)
Yes. Solomon banishes Abiathar and “thus fulfilled the word that the LORD had spoken at Shiloh against the house of Eli.” (1 Kings 2:27) That's a promise kept, and the text says so plainly.
Not this time. The text says the word was spoken at Shiloh “against the house of Eli.” (1 Kings 2:27)
Not quite, friend. The text names a different house. The word spoken at Shiloh was “against the house of Eli.” (1 Kings 2:27)

explanations.answer: To the tent of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Right. Joab “fled to the tent of the LORD.” (1 Kings 2:28) That's where he goes the moment the news reaches him.
Not quite. The text doesn't send Joab to Hebron. He “fled to the tent of the LORD.” (1 Kings 2:28)
Not this time, friend. Joab doesn't head for the river. He “fled to the tent of the LORD.” (1 Kings 2:28)
True. Joab “took hold of the horns of the altar.” (1 Kings 2:28) The text says he went to the tent of the LORD and was beside the altar. (1 Kings 2:29)
It's actually true. The text says Joab fled to the tent of the LORD and “took hold of the horns of the altar.” (1 Kings 2:28)
Yes. Joab answers, “No, I will die here.” (1 Kings 2:30) Benaiah carries that answer back to the king, and Solomon says, “Do just as he says.” (1 Kings 2:31)

explanations.answer: Let me speak to the king
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Joab doesn't ask for a word with Solomon. He says, “No, I will die here.” (1 Kings 2:30)
Not this time. The text has no request for more time. Joab says, “No, I will die here.” (1 Kings 2:30)
That's right. Solomon says Joab struck down those two men “without the knowledge of my father David.” (1 Kings 2:32) Abner and Amasa were both army commanders.
Not quite, friend. Solomon doesn't bring up the priests here. He says Joab acted “without the knowledge of my father David.” (1 Kings 2:32)
Not this time. The elders aren't mentioned in this part. Solomon says it was “without the knowledge of my father David.” (1 Kings 2:32)
True. Solomon says Joab struck down “two men more righteous and better than he.” (1 Kings 2:32) Those men are Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. I think this is a heavy part of the chapter.
It's actually true. Solomon says Abner and Amasa were “more righteous and better than he,” meaning Joab. (1 Kings 2:32) Those are his exact words.

Not quite, friend. It goes the other way. Solomon says, “Their blood will come back upon the heads of Joab and his descendants forever.” (1 Kings 2:33) For David and his house, he says there will be peace from the LORD.

Right, it's false. Solomon says the blood of Abner and Amasa “will come back upon the heads of Joab and his descendants forever.” (1 Kings 2:33) For David, his descendants, his house, and his throne, he says, “there shall be peace from the LORD forever.”

That's him. The king “appointed Benaiah son of Jehoiada in Joab's place over the army.” (1 Kings 2:35) He's the same man who struck down Adonijah and Joab. He went from running the king's errands to running the whole army.
Not quite, friend. The text says Solomon appointed Benaiah son of Jehoiada over the army in Joab's place. (1 Kings 2:35) Benaiah is the one Solomon has been sending out all chapter.
Not this time. The king gives Joab's old job to Benaiah son of Jehoiada. (1 Kings 2:35) Benaiah is the man who carried out Solomon's orders in this chapter.

Not quite. Solomon tells Shimei, who once cursed David (1 Kings 2:8), “Build a house for yourself in Jerusalem and live there, but do not go anywhere else.” (1 Kings 2:36) His days of wandering are over.

Right, it's false. Solomon tells Shimei, “Build a house for yourself in Jerusalem and live there, but do not go anywhere else.” (1 Kings 2:36) Shimei is the man who called down curses on David. (1 Kings 2:8)
Yes. Solomon says, “On the day you go out and cross the Kidron Valley, know for sure that you will die; your blood will be on your own head.” (1 Kings 2:37) He says it plainly, with no wiggle room.
Not quite, friend. Solomon is much more serious than that. He says, “know for sure that you will die.” (1 Kings 2:37)

explanations.answer: He will be put in chains
explanations.explanation: Not this time. No chains in this warning. Solomon says, “know for sure that you will die; your blood will be on your own head.” (1 Kings 2:37)
Right. Shimei says, “The sentence is fair… Your servant will do as my lord the king has spoken.” (1 Kings 2:38) Keep those words in your pocket, because they come back.
Not quite, friend. The text never has Shimei begging. He says, “The sentence is fair.” (1 Kings 2:38)
Not this time. Shimei doesn't ask for time. He answers, “The sentence is fair,” and says he'll do what the king said. (1 Kings 2:38)

explanations.answer: He saddles his donkey and goes after them
explanations.explanation: That's what happens. “Shimei saddled his donkey and set out to Achish at Gath in search of his slaves.” (1 Kings 2:40) That's like seeing a notification and tapping it before you think. I think he forgot that line by the Kidron Valley, because the text doesn't say a word about him pausing.

explanations.answer: He sends a servant to bring them back
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The text says Shimei himself saddled his donkey and set out to Gath. (1 Kings 2:40) No servant is sent in his place.

explanations.answer: He asks the king for permission to go
explanations.explanation: Not this time. The text never has Shimei going to Solomon first. He “saddled his donkey and set out to Achish at Gath.” (1 Kings 2:40)
True. Shimei “brought them back from Gath.” (1 Kings 2:40) The trip worked, but Solomon hears about it. (1 Kings 2:41)
It's actually true. The text says Shimei went to Gath “in search of his slaves, and he brought them back from Gath.” (1 Kings 2:40) The trip itself was a success.
Yes. Solomon asks, “why have you not kept your oath to the LORD and the command that I gave you?” (1 Kings 2:43) He reminds Shimei that he swore by the LORD. (1 Kings 2:42)
Not quite, friend. Solomon doesn't name a promise to David here. He asks why Shimei hasn't kept “your oath to the LORD and the command that I gave you.” (1 Kings 2:43)
Not this time. Solomon doesn't bring up any deal with Achish. He asks about Shimei's “oath to the LORD.” (1 Kings 2:43)
True. Solomon says, “King Solomon will be blessed and David's throne will remain secure before the LORD forever.” (1 Kings 2:45) That's the last thing he says before he gives the command.
It's actually true. Solomon tells Shimei that “David's throne will remain secure before the LORD forever.” (1 Kings 2:45) He also says King Solomon will be blessed.
True. The chapter ends, “Thus the kingdom was firmly established in the hand of Solomon.” (1 Kings 2:46) It was a hard road to get there, friend.
It's actually true. The last line says, “Thus the kingdom was firmly established in the hand of Solomon.” (1 Kings 2:46)
